newsitem.title: PERU: Peru mourns hostage judge killed in assault.
newsitem.headline: Peru mourns hostage judge killed in assault.

text.p: Peru mourned on Wednesday for Supreme Court Justice Carlos Giusti, the only one of 72 hostages to die during a dramatic assault on the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima on Tuesday.

Giusti, described by relatives as a talkative, sociable man, was hit in the leg by a bullet in the shootout between Marxist rebels and crack Peruvian troops and died of a subsequent heart attack, a tearful President Alberto Fujimori announced.
Giusti had been captured along with hundreds of other guests by Marxist rebels during a lavish cocktail party at the residence on Dec. 17.
The rebels released most of their captives early on, but held on to Giusti and others whom they considered most valuable as bargaining chips for their demands.

During the 126 days he spent inside the residence Guisti, who left three children, "spent his time writing and reading a lot," his wife, Iris de Giusti, said in a March 17 interview with local television.
Named a Supreme Court justice in 1993, Giusti would be sorely missed, colleagues said.

"He was always very straightforward. It's really a great loss," one told a local radio station after hearing of his death. "He would arrive at the court and greet everybody, from the cleaner to the judges."
Friends and relatives marked Giusti's 56th birthday on Jan. 26 with Mexican mariachi musicians outside the walls of the diplomatic compound.
His body was taken late on Tuesday to a nearby church and was to be given a formal wake at the Palace of Justice in downtown Lima later on Wednesday.
Two soldiers and the 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels also died in Tuesday's surprise attack.
